title: Parshas Lech Lecha Story for Kids: Avram's Journey
description: A read-aloud Parshas Lech Lecha story for kids: Avram leaves home for Eretz Canaan, rescues Lot and hears Hashem's promise. Plus questions to ask.
keywords: parshas lech lecha story for kids
intro:
Parshas Lech Lecha is the story of the first Yid who followed Hashem into the unknown. Avram leaves his land, his family and everything familiar, because Hashem asks him to. Below is the whole parsha told as a read-aloud story for children aged about 4 to 9, followed by a short section for parents with the main lesson and questions to ask.

It takes about ten minutes to read aloud, which makes it a good fit for the Shabbos table, bedtime, or a quiet Friday afternoon.

sections.heading: Hashem Says: Lech Lecha, Go!
sections.html:
Long, long ago, in a city called Charan, there lived a man named Avram and his wife Sarai. All around them, people bowed down to idols made of wood and stone. But Avram knew a secret that almost nobody else knew. The whole world had one Creator, Hashem, and only Hashem should be served.

One day Hashem spoke to Avram. "Lech lecha," Hashem said. "Go away from your land, from the place you were born, and from your father's house, to the land that I will show you."

Hashem did not even say where the land was. He only promised: "I will make you into a great nation. I will bless you, and through you all the families of the earth will be blessed."

Rashi tells us that the words lech lecha mean "go for yourself," for your own good. Hashem was not sending Avram away to make him sad. Hashem was sending him toward something wonderful.

sections.heading: Packing Up and Setting Out
sections.html:
Can you imagine packing up your whole house to go somewhere you have never seen? Avram did not argue and did not wait. He took Sarai, and his nephew Lot, and all the people who had come to learn about Hashem from them, and they set off.

The Torah calls those people "the souls they made in Charan." Chazal explain that Avram taught the men about Hashem and Sarai taught the women, and it was as if they had made them into new people.

Step by step, across long dusty roads, they walked until they reached the land of Canaan. There Hashem appeared to Avram again and said, "To your children I will give this land." Avram built a mizbeach to thank Hashem. Wherever he went, he built a mizbeach and called out in Hashem's Name, so that everyone would know about Him.

sections.heading: A Hungry Land and a Journey to Mitzrayim
sections.html:
Soon after they arrived, something hard happened. There was a famine in Canaan. The crops did not grow and there was not enough food.

Avram could have complained: "Hashem, You told me to come here, and now there is nothing to eat?" But he did not complain. Chazal count this as one of Avram's tests, and he passed it with emunah. He traveled down to Mitzrayim, where there was food, trusting that Hashem was with him.

In Mitzrayim, Hashem protected Avram and Sarai from the wicked Pharaoh. When the famine was over they came back to Canaan with many animals, silver and gold, and Avram went right back to the mizbeach he had built before, to thank Hashem again.

sections.heading: Avram and Lot Go Separate Ways
sections.html:
Avram and Lot now had so many sheep and cattle that there was not enough grass for all of them. Lot's shepherds began to quarrel with Avram's shepherds.

Avram did not want any fighting in his family. He said to Lot, "Please, let there be no quarrel between us, for we are brothers. The whole land is in front of you. If you go left, I will go right. If you go right, I will go left."

Lot looked out and saw the green, well-watered plain near the city of Sedom. He chose it for himself, even though the people of Sedom were very wicked. Avram stayed in Canaan, and Hashem told him, "Lift up your eyes and look north, south, east and west. All the land that you see, I will give to you and your children forever."

sections.heading: The War of the Kings
sections.html:
One day, four powerful kings went to war against five other kings, and the king of Sedom was one of them. The four kings won. They took away the people of Sedom and all their belongings, and Lot was captured too.

When Avram heard that his nephew had been taken, he did not say, "Lot chose to live in Sedom, it is his own problem." He gathered 318 of his trained men and chased after the kings all through the night. With Hashem's help, Avram's small group defeated the mighty armies and rescued Lot and all the captives.

Malki-Tzedek, the king of Shalem, came out with bread and wine and blessed Avram: "Blessed be Avram to Hashem, Owner of heaven and earth."

The king of Sedom offered Avram all the treasure. But Avram answered, "I will not take even a thread or a shoelace from you, so that you will never say, I made Avram rich." Avram wanted everyone to know that everything he had came from Hashem.

sections.heading: Count the Stars
sections.html:
Even with all his blessings, Avram and Sarai had no children, and they longed for a child.

One night Hashem took Avram outside and said, "Look up at the sky and count the stars, if you can count them. So will your children be." Avram looked up at the countless twinkling stars, and he believed Hashem completely. The Torah tells us that Hashem counted Avram's trust as tzedakah.

Hashem also made a special promise called the Bris Bein HaBesarim. He told Avram that his children would one day be strangers in a land that was not theirs, but in the end they would go free with great wealth and come back to this land.

sections.heading: A Son Named Yishmael
sections.html: Sarai still had no children. So she asked Avram to marry Hagar, her maidservant, hoping that through Hagar the family would grow. Hagar had a son, and an angel told her to call him Yishmael, which means "Hashem will hear." Avram was 86 years old when Yishmael was born.

sections.heading: New Names and the Mitzvah of Bris Milah
sections.html:
When Avram was 99 years old, Hashem appeared to him again. "Walk before Me and be complete," Hashem said. Hashem gave Avram a new name: Avraham, because he would be the father of many nations. Sarai's name became Sarah.

Then Hashem gave Avraham a very special mitzvah, the mitzvah of bris milah. It would be a sign forever between Hashem and Avraham's children. That very day, Avraham did the mitzvah, together with Yishmael and every boy and man in his household. He did not wait even one day.

And Hashem made the most wonderful promise of all: "Sarah your wife will have a son, and you will call him Yitzchak." Avraham was so happy he laughed. The long journey that began with two words, lech lecha, was leading to the beginning of the Jewish people.

sections.heading: For Parents: The Lesson of Lech Lecha
sections.html:
The heart of this parsha is trust. Hashem asks Avram to go without telling him where, and Avram goes. When the land turns out to have a famine, he still trusts. When he has no children, he looks at the stars and believes.

Children face their own small "lech lecha" moments: a new class, a new home, a first night away, a new baby in the family. You can tell them that Avraham Avinu felt what they feel, and he took the first step anyway because he knew Hashem was with him.

Three questions to ask your child:

  1. Hashem did not tell Avram where he was going. How do you think Avram felt? What helped him go anyway?
  2. Avram told Lot, "Let there be no quarrel between us." What can you say when you and a brother, sister or friend are about to fight?
  3. Avram would not take even a shoelace from the king of Sedom. Why did he care so much?

faq.q: What is Parshas Lech Lecha about, in simple words?
faq.a: Hashem tells Avram to leave his home and go to the land He will show him. Avram travels to Canaan, rescues his nephew Lot, receives Hashem's promise of many children and the land, and at the end of the parsha receives the mitzvah of bris milah and the new name Avraham.
Lech lecha means "go for yourself." Rashi explains it as go for your own benefit and good, because the journey would bring Avram blessing.

faq.q: What age is this Lech Lecha story for?
faq.a: It is written for children of about 4 to 9. For younger children you can read just the first two sections and the stars section, and for older children add the questions at the end.

faq.q: What are the main lessons of Lech Lecha for children?
faq.a: Trusting Hashem even when we cannot see the whole path, keeping peace in the family the way Avram did with Lot, helping someone in trouble, and remembering that everything we have comes from Hashem.
